problemTypes.title: Successive percentage change, discount chains and population growth
recipe: Turn each change into a multiplier: +r% becomes 1 + r/100 and −r% becomes 1 − r/100.
Multiply the multipliers in order; starting from 100 keeps the arithmetic in whole numbers.
Read the net change as product − 1, and check its sign against the question's wording (increase or decrease).
problemTypes.trap: Adding the percentages: +20% and −20% is a 4% decrease, not zero.

problemTypes.title: Combined work with someone joining or leaving
recipe: Set total work = LCM of the individual times and turn each person or pipe into units per day (negative for a leak).
Multiply the combined rate by the time worked together to get the work done in that phase.
Divide the remaining units by the rate of whoever is still working.
problemTypes.trap: Adding days instead of rates, or forgetting that the second phase starts from the work left over.

problemTypes.title: Trains, boats and meeting points through relative speed
recipe: Convert every speed to the unit of the distance (× 5/18 for km/h to m/s).
Add speeds for opposite directions and subtract for the same direction; for boats use b ± s.
The distance is the sum of lengths for train-crossing-train, train + platform for a platform, and the gap for meeting problems; time = distance / relative speed.
problemTypes.trap: Leaving speed in km/h while lengths are in metres, which is off by a factor of 3.6.

problemTypes.title: Mixtures: alligation, adding water and replacement
recipe: Identify the component whose amount does not change (milk when water is added).
Use the target percentage to find the new total, then subtract the old total for the amount added.
For two mixtures, place the qualities and the mean in an alligation cross and read the ratio as (c₂ − m) : (m − c₁).
problemTypes.trap: Applying the target percentage to the old total instead of the new one.

problemTypes.title: Probability by counting and by the complement
recipe: Decide whether order matters; when drawing a handful together, count with nCr in both numerator and denominator.
For 'at least one', compute P(none) and subtract from 1.
For a condition (given that ...), restrict the sample space or apply Bayes with a two-branch tree.
problemTypes.trap: Counting ordered draws in the numerator but unordered draws in the denominator.

problemTypes.title: Reading a table, bar chart or pie chart and comparing shares
recipe: Note the units and scale, and for a pie chart the total that the 360° stands for.
Compute only what each option needs: percentage change against the earlier value, share against the column total.
Estimate first and compute exactly only when two options are close.
problemTypes.trap: Taking percentage change on the later year's value, or comparing two pie charts with different totals by angle.

problemTypes.title: Melting and recasting solids, painting surfaces
recipe: Write the volume (for recasting) or the surface area (for painting) of the original solid.
Write the same quantity for one new piece.
Divide, cancelling π before evaluating; if the answer must be an integer, a non-integer means a slip.
problemTypes.trap: Using the cone's slant height in the volume formula, or forgetting the ⅓ in the cone's volume.

problemTypes.title: Averages after adding or removing values, combined means and standard deviation
recipe: Turn every average into a sum: sum = mean × count.
Add or subtract the sums and the counts, then divide; for two groups weight each mean by its size.
For spread, find the mean, then σ² = mean of squares − square of mean; a shift leaves σ alone and scaling by k multiplies it by |k|.
problemTypes.trap: Averaging two group means without weighting by group size, or reporting the variance (or the n − 1 sample SD) when the population SD is asked.

questions.stem: The price of an article is first raised by 30% and then reduced by 30%. Compared with the original price, the final price is
questions.explanation: Multiplier method: 1.30 × 0.70 = 0.91, so the final price is 91% of the original, a 9% decrease. The formula gives the same: 30 − 30 + (30)(−30)/100 = −9. The changes do not cancel because the 30% cut is taken on the larger, raised price.

questions.stem: Two trains, 150 m and 100 m long, run on parallel tracks in the same direction at 60 km/h and 30 km/h. How long does the faster train take to pass the slower one completely?
questions.explanation: Same direction, so the relative speed is 60 − 30 = 30 km/h = 30 × 5/18 = 25/3 m/s. To pass completely, the faster train must cover both lengths, 150 + 100 = 250 m. Time = 250 ÷ (25/3) = 30 s. 10 s is the answer for opposite directions, where the speeds add to 25 m/s.

questions.stem: For a sum lent for 3 years at 10% per annum, the compound interest (compounded annually) exceeds the simple interest by Rs 31. What is the sum, in rupees?
questions.explanation: Per rupee, CI over 3 years is 1.1³ − 1 = 0.331 and SI is 3 × 0.1 = 0.300, so the difference is 0.031 per rupee. The same comes from the formula P(R/100)²(3 + R/100) = P × 0.01 × 3.1 = 0.031P. Setting 0.031P = 31 gives P = 1000.

questions.stem: A can finish a job in 10 days and B in 15 days. They work together for 3 days, after which B leaves. In how many more days does A finish the job?
questions.explanation: Take the job as LCM(10, 15) = 30 units. A does 3 units a day and B 2, so together they do 5 a day and finish 15 units in 3 days. The remaining 15 units at A's 3 units a day take 5 days. 7.5 comes from dividing the remainder by B's rate, and 6 is the time for the whole job working together.

questions.stem: A 60-litre mixture of milk and water is 75% milk. How many litres of water must be added so that milk makes up 60% of the mixture?
questions.explanation: Milk = 0.75 × 60 = 45 L, and adding water does not change it. For milk to be 60% of the new total, the total must be 45/0.6 = 75 L. Water to add = 75 − 60 = 15 L.

questions.stem: What is the next term of the series 1, 8, 9, 64, 25, 216, … ?
questions.explanation: The terms alternate between squares of odd positions and cubes of even positions: 1², 2³, 3², 4³, 5², 6³. The seventh term is an odd position, so it is 7² = 49. 343 = 7³ comes from assuming the cube–square pattern continues the wrong way.

questions.stem: A bag holds 3 green and 4 red balls. Two balls are drawn together at random. What is the probability that at least one of them is green? (Answer to 2 decimals)
questions.explanation: Complement: P(no green) = P(both red) = C(4,2)/C(7,2) = 6/21 = 2/7. So P(at least one green) = 1 − 2/7 = 5/7 ≈ 0.714. Direct count gives the same: (C(3,1)C(4,1) + C(3,2))/21 = (12 + 3)/21 = 15/21.

questions.stem: Machine A makes 60% of a factory's bolts and machine B the rest. 2% of A's bolts and 5% of B's bolts are defective. A bolt picked at random is defective. What is the probability that machine B made it?
questions.explanation: P(defective) = 0.6 × 0.02 + 0.4 × 0.05 = 0.012 + 0.020 = 0.032. By Bayes, P(B | defective) = 0.020/0.032 = 5/8. 3/8 is P(A | defective), and 2/5 is the prior share of B, ignoring the evidence.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements are true?
options: $\log(a + b) = \log a + \log b$ for all positive a and b
The binary representation of 1000 has exactly 10 bits
questions.explanation: (A) 2¹⁰ = 1024, true. (B) false: the product rule is log(ab) = log a + log b; for a = b = 1, log 2 ≠ 0. (C) 2⁹ = 512 ≤ 1000 < 1024, so ⌊log₂ 1000⌋ + 1 = 10 bits, true. (D) log₈ 4 = log₂ 4 / log₂ 8 = 2/3, not 3/2; the option inverts the change of base.

questions.stem: In how many ways can the letters of the word SPEAK be arranged so that the two vowels are always next to each other?
questions.explanation: Glue E and A into one block. The units are S, P, K and [EA], which can be arranged in 4! = 24 ways, and the block itself can be EA or AE, giving 24 × 2 = 48. 24 forgets the internal order; 120 = 5! ignores the condition; 72 = 120 − 48 counts the arrangements where the vowels are apart.

questions.stem: A solid metal sphere of radius 6 cm is melted and recast into solid cones, each of base radius 3 cm and height 4 cm, with no loss of metal. How many cones are made?
questions.explanation: Volume of the sphere = (4/3)π × 6³ = 288π cm³. Volume of one cone = (1/3)π × 3² × 4 = 12π cm³. Number of cones = 288π / 12π = 24. Forgetting the ⅓ in the cone formula gives 8.

questions.stem: A triangle has sides 13 cm, 14 cm and 15 cm. What is the radius of its circumscribed circle, in cm? (Answer to 3 decimals)
questions.explanation: Heron: s = 21 and A = √(21 × 8 × 7 × 6) = √7056 = 84 cm². Circumradius R = abc/(4A) = (13 × 14 × 15)/(4 × 84) = 2730/336 = 8.125 cm. The inradius, A/s = 4, is the usual wrong pick, and 7.5 is half the longest side, which equals R only in a right triangle; here 13² + 14² = 365 ≠ 15² = 225.

questions.stem: A company's revenue (in crore rupees) from four products was P 40, Q 25, R 60, S 75 in Year 1, and P 50, Q 30, R 54, S 66 in Year 2. Which of the following statements are true?
options: P had the largest percentage increase from Year 1 to Year 2
Total revenue was the same in both years
R's share of total revenue in Year 2 was more than 25%
S's revenue fell by more than 15% from Year 1 to Year 2
questions.explanation: Percentage changes on the Year 1 values: P +10/40 = +25%, Q +5/25 = +20%, R −6/60 = −10%, S −9/75 = −12%. (A) true. (B) totals are 40 + 25 + 60 + 75 = 200 and 50 + 30 + 54 + 66 = 200, true. (C) 54/200 = 27%, true. (D) S fell 12%, not more than 15%, false. Taking S's change on the Year 2 value (9/66 ≈ 13.6%) still does not exceed 15%.

questions.stem: On a map drawn to the scale 1 : 2,50,000, town B is 6 cm due east of town A, and town C is 8 cm due north of B. What is the straight-line ground distance from A to C, in km?
questions.explanation: The legs AB and BC are perpendicular, so the map distance AC = √(6² + 8²) = 10 cm. At 1 : 2,50,000, 1 cm on the map is 2,50,000 cm = 2.5 km on the ground, so AC = 10 × 2.5 = 25 km. Adding the legs instead (14 cm) gives 35 km, and reading 1 cm as 25 km gives 250.

questions.stem: What is the population standard deviation (dividing by n) of the data 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9?
questions.explanation: Mean = 40/8 = 5. Squared deviations: 9, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 4, 16, which sum to 32. Population variance = 32/8 = 4, so σ = 2. 4 is the variance, not the SD. 2.14 ≈ √(32/7) is the sample SD, which divides by n − 1.

questions.stem: A fair coin is tossed 4 times, and X is the number of heads. Which of the following statements are true?
questions.explanation: X is binomial with n = 4 and p = ½. (A) P(X = 2) = C(4, 2)/2⁴ = 6/16 = 3/8, true. (B) E[X] = np = 2, true. (C) Var(X) = np(1 − p) = 4 × ½ × ½ = 1, not 2, false; 2 is the mean. (D) P(X ≥ 1) = 1 − P(no heads) = 1 − 1/16 = 15/16, true. Listing all 16 outcomes confirms each value.

pitfalls.text: Unit mismatch: lengths in metres with speeds in km/h, or a rate per hour against a time in minutes. Convert everything to one unit system first.
Assuming +x% and −x% cancel. The second change acts on the new base, so the net is always a loss of x²/100 percent.
Adding days in time-and-work problems. Add rates (1/a + 1/b), or use the LCM-units method.
Summing 1, 2, 3, … successes for an 'at least one' probability when 1 − P(none) takes one line.
Ignoring the scale or units on a chart's axis (thousands versus millions, percent versus absolute) and answering a different question than the one asked.
Averaging speeds arithmetically over equal distances. The average is 2uv/(u + v), which is always below (u + v)/2 unless u = v.
Mixing up P(A | B) and P(B | A) in Bayes questions, or quoting the prior share as the answer and ignoring the evidence.
Using slant height l in a cone's volume or vertical height h in its curved surface. Volume uses h, curved surface uses l = √(r² + h²).
